_what: Real (APK class, linejs entry) pairings the ungated extractor acted on, with both sides' field or member names as extracted. `expect` is the verdict the gates must reach; `why` records what the pairing really was.

structPairings.why: R8 named a shop-product class and a chatapp result class both `h`; the RPC binding is keyed by short name and picked the wrong one. Eight field renames followed.
Same collision: a billing struct bound onto a group-call route, which then acquired billingItemId and unavailableItemPurchase.
Disjoint two-field structs. Unique on both sides, so shape uniqueness alone let this through before the content floor existed.
LINE does not obfuscate this package, so the name is an identity. The one struct field add that survived gating on 26.14.0.
A content-only pairing on a wide struct: high overlap across many shared names. Trusted enough to correct a slot both sides already have, not enough to invent one.
Overlap 1.00 on two generic names. LINE ships many {language, country} structs, so a perfect score here says 'both are small', not 'both are Locale'. Applying it moved Locale's field ids.
One shared name, and that name is `request`. Every _args struct in LINE matches this at 1.00.
A field renamed at the same id and type on a wide struct — real drift, corroborated by everything around it.

enumPairings.why: 123 members. No second enum in LINE shares this many member names by accident.
6 members. Held for review: too small for a name overlap to mean anything.
A two-member {ANDROID, IOS} enum matches every other two-member {ANDROID, IOS} enum at Jaccard 1.0 — and this one had the ordinals swapped.

_names: apkNames/linejsNames are representative samples, not the full sets: each keeps the observed overlap ratio and enough of the shared names to land in the same band as the real pairing, so the gates see equivalent evidence without 100+ literals per case.
